html:
SMTO-HTTP-0003 — Signing in to the service took too long

GUID: 94dec685-5781-4839-97d0-c886f37ee085
Slug: http-auth-timeout
Domain: HTTP · Subsystem: http

What happened

  • Before sending your request, SMTO tried to sign in to the service, but the sign-in didn't finish in time. Your main request wasn't sent.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Check that the service is up, for example by opening its sign-in page in a browser on the Gateway computer the connection uses. If the service itself is down or very slow, no setting in SMTO will make the sign-in finish.
  2. Open Parameter Store, select this HTTP Connection, and check that Login path or Token endpoint points to the right address. A wrong address can hang instead of failing quickly.
  3. If the service is just slow, raise Test timeout (seconds) for tests, or ask SMTO in the conversation to allow more time for the request (up to 120 seconds). The sign-in shares the request's time limit; changing the Model's timeout settings doesn't affect it.
  4. Select Test connection. The test shows whether the sign-in now finishes within its time limit.

What success looks like

  • Test connection reports Reachable and Authenticated, and your request completes.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages the service or this HTTP Connection. Don't turn off TLS certificate verification or other security settings; that won't make the service answer faster.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • HTTP authentication exceeded the request deadline, or Requests raised a timeout, while contacting the login or token endpoint, before the resource request.

What this means

  • The authentication deadline expired before an exchange or Requests raised a timeout while contacting the login endpoint. The specific receipt owns dispatch and effect truth. Authentication exchanges, resource requests and Gateway admission are separate phases; rendering this explanation performs no request and never authorizes replay of an uncertain mutation.

Why this can happen

  • The authentication deadline expired before an exchange or Requests raised a timeout while contacting the login endpoint.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect authentication attempt count and endpoint execution evidence to distinguish no exchange from a login that may have reached the server.

How to fix it

  • The auth exchange shares the resource request's deadline (http.request timeout_seconds, default 30 and at most 120, or the profile's test timeout, at most 30). Check the login or token endpoint's availability and latency from the Gateway host; raise the request or test timeout only if the endpoint is healthy but slow. Model timeout settings do not apply to login requests.
  • Check the login endpoint health and HTTP authentication timeout; model timeout settings do not own login requests.

Retry and execution caution

  • Apply the correction and confirm the relevant state before requesting another attempt. Prior completed work remains governed by its receipts.

How to verify the fix

  • A bounded authentication exchange finishes within its own deadline and establishes the intended session.

What not to do

  • Do not remove retained state or weaken trust checks to make an unavailable dependency appear healthy.

Technical notes

  • The specific receipt owns dispatch and effect truth. Authentication exchanges, resource requests and Gateway admission are separate phases; rendering this explanation performs no request and never authorizes replay of an uncertain mutation.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
